findings.source_quote: παντὸς οὐδήποτε ἐντὸς ὅρων θεοσεβείας ὄντος
findings.english_quote: The selected print has smooth-breathed οὐδήποτε, which ordinarily means “never” and does not fit the genitive construction with παντός and ὄντος.
findings.issue: The note incorrectly dismisses the printed negative reading as incompatible with the genitive construction. Substantival παντός can participate in a genitive absolute, and an adverb meaning “never” can modify ὄντος. Consequently, a reading concerning someone who is never within the bounds of reverence for God is syntactically possible, although contextually difficult. The positive main rendering is defensible through the explicitly proposed indefinite reading οὑδήποτε, but the note does not fairly disclose the materially different negative construction.
findings.suggested_revision: Revise the note to acknowledge the syntactic possibility of the supplied negative reading, with an alternative such as “any person who is never within the bounds of reverence for God.” Explain why the surrounding account of reverence, nonblasphemy, and innate longing favors interpreting the printed breathing as an orthographic anomaly and proposing οὑδήποτε, “of anyone whatsoever.” Keep that proposal distinct from the confirmed supplied reading. This requires interpretive disclosure, not renewed verification of the already image-checked print; submit the amended passage and note for fresh review.

findings.source_quote: δύνασθε δὲ ὁμοίως τὸ δεύτερον, διὰ τῆς μετανοίας (ὡς ἔφην) τὰ θεῷ ἀρέσκοντα ἀναδεξάμενοι καὶ τὰ σώματα ἀναρρῶσαι καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἀναλαβεῖν.
findings.english_quote: But in the same way you can, a second time, through repentance—as I said—accept the things pleasing to God and both restore your bodies to health and recover your souls.
findings.issue: The draft turns the subordinate participle ἀναδεξάμενοι into another infinitive governed by “you can.” In the Greek, accepting what pleases God supplies the circumstance or means under which bodily restoration and recovery of the souls are possible; δύνασθε directly governs ἀναρρῶσαι and ἀναλαβεῖν. The English instead coordinates the ability to accept with the ability to restore and recover, weakening the stated relationship and expanding the modal claim.
findings.suggested_revision: Restore the subordinate relationship, for example: “But likewise, a second time, through repentance—as I said—by accepting what pleases God, you can both restore your bodies to health and recover your souls.” Review this proposed replacement afresh before acceptance.
